title: The Loop-Variable Closure Trap and Two Fixes
description: See why closures created in a comprehension share one loop-variable binding, and compare fixing it with a default parameter versus a factory function.
source: draft: agy free model + edit: codex

steps.description: Line 2 builds `fns = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]`, where all three lambdas close over the single comprehension variable `i`. By the time `[f() for f in fns]` calls them on line 3, the loop has finished with `i = 2`. Line 3 prints `[2, 2, 2]`; outside the comprehension on lines 8-11, `i` is out of scope and prints `not available`.

Line 14 writes `fns_fixed1 = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]`. Python evaluates the default argument `i=i` when each `lambda` is defined, binding each function's own parameter `i` to `0`, `1`, and `2` in turn.
Lines 18-21 define `make_fn(i)` and call `[make_fn(i) for i in range(3)]`. Each call to `make_fn(i)` creates a separate call frame with its own `i` parameter for `lambda: i` to capture.
Compare line 2 with lines 14 and 18-21: line 2 creates one `i` binding shared by all three lambdas, whereas lines 14 and 18-21 create a distinct `i` binding on each iteration.

steps.question: When `[f() for f in fns_fixed1]` on line 15 and `[f() for f in fns_fixed2]` on line 22 run, what list does each print?
steps.answer: Both print `[0, 1, 2]`, because each lambda reads its own per-iteration binding (`0`, `1`, and `2`).

steps.description: Inside `make_fn(0)`, line 19 returns a `lambda: i` whose enclosing frame holds `i = 0`. That frame is separate from the frames that `make_fn(1)` and `make_fn(2)` will create.
